title: Amorphous/crystalline HTiNbO_5-X membranes for efficient confined flow synthesis of acetate ester flavours

paper_content.introduction:
Efficient,environmental,andeconomicallyviablechemicalprocessesormethodologiesareingreatdemandforthosewidelyusedorganiccompounds. Confinementcanplayadefiningroleininterfacepropertiesandchemical catalysis6. As the materials are assembled/confined to nanoscale,theirgeometricandelectronicstructuresintheconfinedstateoperateasthermodynamicallyandkineticallymorecriticalfactorsthanthoseinthebulkstate,whichcanresultinunusualphysicochemical and catalytic properties7. Over the past decade, tremendouseffortshavebeendevotedtopreparingvariousporousnanomaterialsfrom1Dto3D(e.g.,carbonnanotubes,grapheneoxide,metal-organicframeworks),whileonlyasmallportionofworkhavesuccessfully constructed nanoconfined systems or materials8–10. For example,Al/Ni-Pt/Tinanotubewasreportedtoshowremarkablyhigh efficiencyinnitrobenzenehydrogenationduetotheinstanttransferofintermediates and the tailored electronic properties of confined nanochannels9.However,thesematerialsmainlyparticipateincatalyticreactionsthroughbatchreactorsandthereactionefficienciesarestilllimitedbythedisorderedmotionofmoleculesandtheinefficientdiffusionofmoleculesbetweenthebulksolutionandthenanochannelsofporousmaterials,especiallyformolecular-scalechannels10. Moreover,currentstudyofcatalyticmaterialsaremainlyfocusedonthedesignofnanomaterialswithhierarchicalchannelsandthedegreeofconfinementforthesesystemsarelocalizedwithinseveraltotensofnanometers considering heat and mass transfer, and thereby the intrinsic structure−activity relationship of sub-nanoscale confinement has attracted intense interests6.

Innaturalenzymes,reactantsdiffuseintotheactivesiteswiththebindingsitesandcatalyticsitestobreakandformbonds11.Thesynergyofmultiple sites contribute to their extremely high activity and selectivity. There is a great challenge to apply this concepts into membrane flow reactors with confined channels in sub-nanometer scale,eventhoughitisattheforefrontofcatalyticchemistry.Recently,many 2D materials, such as graphene oxide (GO), covalent organic framework (COF), layered double hydroxide (LDH), and transition metal oxides/chalcogenides (TMO/C), have been employed for the fabrication of 2D material membranes, and these membranes have been effectively practiced in separation and purification12–16.Actually,2Dmaterialshaveatomic-levelthicknessesanduniquephysicochemicalproperties,andtheyarealsoverypromisingplatformstodevelopnewnanoconfinedflowreactorsfororganicsynthesis17,18.Forinstance,we have controlled the chemical structure of 2D graphene oxide membraneseffectively,andrealizedrapidKnoevenagelcondensationand synthesis of aspirin recently19,20. Through tuning the interlayer distances and interface properties of nanochannels, the intrinsic characteristicsof the reaction, e.g.,mass transfer,reaction kinetics, and selectivity, can be effectively dominated under mild process conditions. It is thus attractive to implement laminar membrane reactorsforcontinuouspharmaceuticalandfinechemicalsynthesis18.However,thedifficultyinpreparingofuniform,largesizedandultrathin 2D nanosheets (e.g., COF, LDH) to create effective confined nanochannelsgreatlyrestrictthedevelopmentofLMR17.Inaddition,thecurrentlyreported2Dmaterialslackproperandstablecatalyticactivesitesforspecificreactions(esterificationinthiswork).Incontrast to 2D carbonaceous materials like GO with abundant oxygen-containinggroups,2Dmetalliccompounds(e.g.,TMO)aredifficultto modulate the microenvironment nearby catalytic sites21. However, achieving precise control of these defects remains a significant challenge, and the role of vacancies to the adsorptionandactivationofreactants,especiallyunder2Dconfinedconditions,remainslargelyunknown23.

The synergy of multiple sites and confined spatial structures are realized in this bioinspiredLMR,contributingtothemodulationofreactantadsorption,molecularpolarization,orbitalsymmetrymatchingandreactionthermodynamics.Wehaveadjustedthemembranethicknesses,pressuredifference, reaction temperatures and reactant concentrations, andfurtherexpandedthesubstratescopeandstabilitytest,proving therationalityandsuperiorityofthelaminarmembranereactorstoconventionalbatchreactors.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Fang et al. present a laminar membrane reactor using HTiNbO5-X nanosheets enriched with oxygen vacancies. This study demonstrates high catalytic performance for the esterification of benzyl alcohol under mild conditions, achieving nearly 100% conversion within 26.6 seconds at 23°C, with a high turnover number of 306.42. The combination of oxygen vacancies and spatial confinement enhances reactant adsorption, improves orbital symmetry matching, and lowers the reaction’s energy barrier, as confirmed by both experimental results and DFT calculations. Additionally, the membrane reactor exhibits long-term stability, maintaining high conversion efficiency over 13 days of continuous use, highlighting its potential for practical applications. Overall, this is an interesting paper, but the following comments and questions should be addressed before this work can be considered for publication in Nature Communications:
• The introduction provides a good background on catalytic materials and the advantages of 2D materials. However, it would be helpful to clearly define the study’s specific objectives and key research questions—particularly regarding the synergistic effects of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement.
• Some technical terms, such as Brønsted acid site modulation and orbital symmetry matching, could benefit from brief explanations for clarity, considering Nature Communications’ broad audience.
• While the DFT analysis is insightful, could the authors also include a kinetic model in Figure 1 that explicitly outlines the rate-limiting steps? This would enhance the mechanistic understanding.
• The manuscript mentions the synergistic effect of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement but doesn’t discuss the actual mechanism. Could the authors provide a more detailed discussion on how these factors influence adsorption, orbital symmetry matching, and energy barrier reduction? A schematic diagram illustrating the proposed mechanism would be beneficial.
• The authors should specify the exact conditions (temperature, duration, and concentration) used in the acid etching and exfoliation steps.
• Have the authors explored regeneration methods after deactivation (e.g., washing or thermal treatment)?
• The comparison with literature values is useful, but a direct catalytic activity comparison (e.g., turnover frequency) against commercial catalysts would strengthen the study’s industrial relevance. Additionally, how does this membrane reactor compare with previously reported catalytic systems such as COFs and LDHs in terms of reaction rates, TOF, and catalyst stability?
• The presented DFT results suggest that decreasing the interlayer distance improves conversion. Have the authors attempted to reduce the interlayer spacing below 11.0 Å?
• The authors should report their synthesis reproducibility (and batch-to-batch variation).
• What is the distribution of the amorphous vs. crystalline phase percentage in the final nanosheets?
• A discussion on how the distribution of Brønsted and Lewis acid sites impacts catalytic performance would be beneficial.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript proposes a concept of using stacked two-dimensional (2D) amorphous/crystalline HTiNbO5−x nanosheets as sub-nanoconfined membrane reactors for the efficient synthesis of acetate ester flavors under mild conditions. The experimental results demonstrate that the esterification of benzyl alcohol achieves nearly 100% conversion within 26.6 seconds when the interlayer spacing is reduced to 11.0 Å, significantly outperforming conventional bulk reactions. The concept has been reported in the previous work (Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2310954; Matter 2023, 6, 1173; Adv. Sci. 2024, 11, 2308388). The manuscript suffers from significant shortcomings in mechanistic explanations, model construction, and experimental validation, which undermine the support for its core scientific claims. As it stands, the manuscript is not suitable for publication.
Detailed Comments
1. Insufficient Mechanistic Explanation and Lack of Direct Evidence
The authors attribute the enhanced performance to the synergistic effect of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement. However, the following issues remain unresolved:
a. Direct Role of Oxygen Vacancies Not Clearly Demonstrated: Although XPS and EPR characterizations suggest the presence of oxygen vacancies, no control experiments (e.g., synthesizing HTiNbO5-x membranes without oxygen vacancies) were conducted to confirm their necessity. Without such experiments, it is impossible to rule out the dominant role of other factors, such as surface acid sites or differences in interlayer mass transport.
b. Lack of Empirical Evidence for Orbital Symmetry Matching: The manuscript claims that HOMO-LUMO symmetry matching (Fig. 1j) is responsible for the accelerated reaction, but no direct evidence (e.g., in situ spectroscopy such as Raman or XAS) is provided. Reliance solely on DFT calculations is insufficient to support this key mechanistic claim.
2. Unclear Theoretical Model Construction
a. Questionable Validity of the Confined Reaction Model: The differences between the DFT models for "confined reaction" and "bulk reaction" are not clearly explained. For instance, when the interlayer spacing is reduced to 4 Å, how is the model's consistency with the actual material structure (e.g., oxygen vacancy distribution, surface functional groups) ensured? Are solvation effects or dynamic adsorption processes considered?
b. Discrepancy Between Computational Parameters and Experimental Conditions: The manuscript does not clarify whether the interlayer spacings used in the calculations (e.g., 40 Å vs. 4 Å) correspond to the experimentally measured XRD data (e.g., 11.0 Å). If the model parameters do not match the experimental conditions, the computational results lose their explanatory power.
3. Limitations in Material Characterization and Reactor Design
a. Lack of Verification of Interlayer Spacing Uniformity: While SEM and XRD data suggest an ordered layered structure, high-resolution characterization (e.g., HAADF-STEM) is needed to confirm the local uniformity of nanosheet stacking. Stacking defects or interlayer inhomogeneity could significantly affect the reproducibility of the reaction.
b. Mass Transport Effects Not Excluded: The experimental results (e.g., the relationship between reaction time and interlayer spacing) may be dominated by mass transport rates rather than catalytic activity. Additional experiments (e.g., varying flow rates at fixed interlayer spacing) are needed to distinguish the contributions of mass transport and catalysis.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors reported the creation of a HTiNbO5-x membrane for esterification of benzyl alcohol with acetic anhydride to yield benzyl acetate and other derivatives (depending on type of benzyl alcohol used). Comprehensive and complementary characterisation techniques were used to provide robust evidence that demonstrated the noteworthy esterification rates and turnover numbers. The mechanism underpinning delivery of such results were evaluated using suitable simulation methodology. Although the research and work merits publication in Nature Communication, there was a major flaw in the design of the experiments. The following questions and comments outline my concerns about experimental design associated with this paper:
1) What is the motivation to develop a membrane for esterification of benzyl alcohol? Existing methods are already well-established and effective. Hence it was unclear why this work is important scientifically or industrially. The only segment of the manuscript that compared the performance of the current membranes with other catalysts was only limited to Lines 230 to 236. There were no analyses on why their membranes are better than existing catalysts beyond catalysis performance.
2) Benzyl alcohol esterification is a well-established process in industry. However, why did the authors not compare outcomes from this work with already established processes? Comparisons were made with catalysts reported in scientific research (mostly used in labs) for e.g., ionic liquids, solid and inorganic acids, but there was no comparison with industrial processes. After all, the authors are in the opinion that their membranes outperform existing methods for benzyl alcohol esterification.
3) Why did the authors use acetonitrile as the solvent and acetic anhydride for esterification in this work? BA is typically esterified in industry using acetic acid (as solvent and reagent for esterification), toluene, or hexane.
4) Are the membranes single use? What is the cyclic catalytic performance of the membranes reported here?
The authors should carefully address these questions to improve the quality of the manuscript that is underpinned by solid, and interesting results before it can be published in Nat. Commun.

### Reviewer 1

Fang et al. present a laminar membrane reactor using HTiNbO5-X nanosheets enriched with oxygen vacancies. This study demonstrates high catalytic performance for the esterification of benzyl alcohol under mild conditions, achieving nearly 100% conversion within 26.6 seconds at 23°C, with a high turnover number of 306.42. The combination of oxygen vacancies and spatial confinement enhances reactant adsorption, improves orbital symmetry matching, and lowers the reaction’s energy barrier, as confirmed by both experimental results and DFT calculations. Additionally, the membrane reactor exhibits long-term stability, maintaining high conversion efficiency over 13 days of continuous use, highlighting its potential for practical applications. Overall, this is an interesting paper, but the following comments and questions should be addressed before this work can be considered for publication in Nature Communications:
• The introduction provides a good background on catalytic materials and the advantages of 2D materials. However, it would be helpful to clearly define the study’s specific objectives and key research questions—particularly regarding the synergistic effects of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement.
• Some technical terms, such as Brønsted acid site modulation and orbital symmetry matching, could benefit from brief explanations for clarity, considering Nature Communications’ broad audience.
• While the DFT analysis is insightful, could the authors also include a kinetic model in Figure 1 that explicitly outlines the rate-limiting steps? This would enhance the mechanistic understanding.
• The manuscript mentions the synergistic effect of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement but doesn’t discuss the actual mechanism. Could the authors provide a more detailed discussion on how these factors influence adsorption, orbital symmetry matching, and energy barrier reduction? A schematic diagram illustrating the proposed mechanism would be beneficial.
• The authors should specify the exact conditions (temperature, duration, and concentration) used in the acid etching and exfoliation steps.
• Have the authors explored regeneration methods after deactivation (e.g., washing or thermal treatment)?
• The comparison with literature values is useful, but a direct catalytic activity comparison (e.g., turnover frequency) against commercial catalysts would strengthen the study’s industrial relevance. Additionally, how does this membrane reactor compare with previously reported catalytic systems such as COFs and LDHs in terms of reaction rates, TOF, and catalyst stability?
• The presented DFT results suggest that decreasing the interlayer distance improves conversion. Have the authors attempted to reduce the interlayer spacing below 11.0 Å?
• The authors should report their synthesis reproducibility (and batch-to-batch variation).
• What is the distribution of the amorphous vs. crystalline phase percentage in the final nanosheets?
• A discussion on how the distribution of Brønsted and Lewis acid sites impacts catalytic performance would be beneficial.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript proposes a concept of using stacked two-dimensional (2D) amorphous/crystalline HTiNbO5−x nanosheets as sub-nanoconfined membrane reactors for the efficient synthesis of acetate ester flavors under mild conditions. The experimental results demonstrate that the esterification of benzyl alcohol achieves nearly 100% conversion within 26.6 seconds when the interlayer spacing is reduced to 11.0 Å, significantly outperforming conventional bulk reactions. The concept has been reported in the previous work (Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2310954; Matter 2023, 6, 1173; Adv. Sci. 2024, 11, 2308388). The manuscript suffers from significant shortcomings in mechanistic explanations, model construction, and experimental validation, which undermine the support for its core scientific claims. As it stands, the manuscript is not suitable for publication.
Detailed Comments
1. Insufficient Mechanistic Explanation and Lack of Direct Evidence
The authors attribute the enhanced performance to the synergistic effect of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement. However, the following issues remain unresolved:
a. Direct Role of Oxygen Vacancies Not Clearly Demonstrated: Although XPS and EPR characterizations suggest the presence of oxygen vacancies, no control experiments (e.g., synthesizing HTiNbO5-x membranes without oxygen vacancies) were conducted to confirm their necessity. Without such experiments, it is impossible to rule out the dominant role of other factors, such as surface acid sites or differences in interlayer mass transport.
b. Lack of Empirical Evidence for Orbital Symmetry Matching: The manuscript claims that HOMO-LUMO symmetry matching (Fig. 1j) is responsible for the accelerated reaction, but no direct evidence (e.g., in situ spectroscopy such as Raman or XAS) is provided. Reliance solely on DFT calculations is insufficient to support this key mechanistic claim.
2. Unclear Theoretical Model Construction
a. Questionable Validity of the Confined Reaction Model: The differences between the DFT models for "confined reaction" and "bulk reaction" are not clearly explained. For instance, when the interlayer spacing is reduced to 4 Å, how is the model's consistency with the actual material structure (e.g., oxygen vacancy distribution, surface functional groups) ensured? Are solvation effects or dynamic adsorption processes considered?
b. Discrepancy Between Computational Parameters and Experimental Conditions: The manuscript does not clarify whether the interlayer spacings used in the calculations (e.g., 40 Å vs. 4 Å) correspond to the experimentally measured XRD data (e.g., 11.0 Å). If the model parameters do not match the experimental conditions, the computational results lose their explanatory power.
3. Limitations in Material Characterization and Reactor Design
a. Lack of Verification of Interlayer Spacing Uniformity: While SEM and XRD data suggest an ordered layered structure, high-resolution characterization (e.g., HAADF-STEM) is needed to confirm the local uniformity of nanosheet stacking. Stacking defects or interlayer inhomogeneity could significantly affect the reproducibility of the reaction.
b. Mass Transport Effects Not Excluded: The experimental results (e.g., the relationship between reaction time and interlayer spacing) may be dominated by mass transport rates rather than catalytic activity. Additional experiments (e.g., varying flow rates at fixed interlayer spacing) are needed to distinguish the contributions of mass transport and catalysis.

### Reviewer 3

The authors reported the creation of a HTiNbO5-x membrane for esterification of benzyl alcohol with acetic anhydride to yield benzyl acetate and other derivatives (depending on type of benzyl alcohol used). Comprehensive and complementary characterisation techniques were used to provide robust evidence that demonstrated the noteworthy esterification rates and turnover numbers. The mechanism underpinning delivery of such results were evaluated using suitable simulation methodology. Although the research and work merits publication in Nature Communication, there was a major flaw in the design of the experiments. The following questions and comments outline my concerns about experimental design associated with this paper:
1) What is the motivation to develop a membrane for esterification of benzyl alcohol? Existing methods are already well-established and effective. Hence it was unclear why this work is important scientifically or industrially. The only segment of the manuscript that compared the performance of the current membranes with other catalysts was only limited to Lines 230 to 236. There were no analyses on why their membranes are better than existing catalysts beyond catalysis performance.
2) Benzyl alcohol esterification is a well-established process in industry. However, why did the authors not compare outcomes from this work with already established processes? Comparisons were made with catalysts reported in scientific research (mostly used in labs) for e.g., ionic liquids, solid and inorganic acids, but there was no comparison with industrial processes. After all, the authors are in the opinion that their membranes outperform existing methods for benzyl alcohol esterification.
3) Why did the authors use acetonitrile as the solvent and acetic anhydride for esterification in this work? BA is typically esterified in industry using acetic acid (as solvent and reagent for esterification), toluene, or hexane.
4) Are the membranes single use? What is the cyclic catalytic performance of the membranes reported here?
The authors should carefully address these questions to improve the quality of the manuscript that is underpinned by solid, and interesting results before it can be published in Nat. Commun.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

Fang et al. present a laminar membrane reactor using HTiNbO5-X nanosheets enriched with oxygen vacancies. This study demonstrates high catalytic performance for the esterification of benzyl alcohol under mild conditions, achieving nearly 100% conversion within 26.6 seconds at 23°C, with a high turnover number of 306.42. The combination of oxygen vacancies and spatial confinement enhances reactant adsorption, improves orbital symmetry matching, and lowers the reaction’s energy barrier, as confirmed by both experimental results and DFT calculations. Additionally, the membrane reactor exhibits long-term stability, maintaining high conversion efficiency over 13 days of continuous use, highlighting its potential for practical applications. Overall, this is an interesting paper, but the following comments and questions should be addressed before this work can be considered for publication in Nature Communications:
• The introduction provides a good background on catalytic materials and the advantages of 2D materials. However, it would be helpful to clearly define the study’s specific objectives and key research questions—particularly regarding the synergistic effects of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement.
• Some technical terms, such as Brønsted acid site modulation and orbital symmetry matching, could benefit from brief explanations for clarity, considering Nature Communications’ broad audience.
• While the DFT analysis is insightful, could the authors also include a kinetic model in Figure 1 that explicitly outlines the rate-limiting steps? This would enhance the mechanistic understanding.
• The manuscript mentions the synergistic effect of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement but doesn’t discuss the actual mechanism. Could the authors provide a more detailed discussion on how these factors influence adsorption, orbital symmetry matching, and energy barrier reduction? A schematic diagram illustrating the proposed mechanism would be beneficial.
• The authors should specify the exact conditions (temperature, duration, and concentration) used in the acid etching and exfoliation steps.
• Have the authors explored regeneration methods after deactivation (e.g., washing or thermal treatment)?
• The comparison with literature values is useful, but a direct catalytic activity comparison (e.g., turnover frequency) against commercial catalysts would strengthen the study’s industrial relevance. Additionally, how does this membrane reactor compare with previously reported catalytic systems such as COFs and LDHs in terms of reaction rates, TOF, and catalyst stability?
• The presented DFT results suggest that decreasing the interlayer distance improves conversion. Have the authors attempted to reduce the interlayer spacing below 11.0 Å?
• The authors should report their synthesis reproducibility (and batch-to-batch variation).
• What is the distribution of the amorphous vs. crystalline phase percentage in the final nanosheets?
• A discussion on how the distribution of Brønsted and Lewis acid sites impacts catalytic performance would be beneficial.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript proposes a concept of using stacked two-dimensional (2D) amorphous/crystalline HTiNbO5−x nanosheets as sub-nanoconfined membrane reactors for the efficient synthesis of acetate ester flavors under mild conditions. The experimental results demonstrate that the esterification of benzyl alcohol achieves nearly 100% conversion within 26.6 seconds when the interlayer spacing is reduced to 11.0 Å, significantly outperforming conventional bulk reactions. The concept has been reported in the previous work (Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2310954; Matter 2023, 6, 1173; Adv. Sci. 2024, 11, 2308388). The manuscript suffers from significant shortcomings in mechanistic explanations, model construction, and experimental validation, which undermine the support for its core scientific claims. As it stands, the manuscript is not suitable for publication.
Detailed Comments
1. Insufficient Mechanistic Explanation and Lack of Direct Evidence
The authors attribute the enhanced performance to the synergistic effect of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement. However, the following issues remain unresolved:
a. Direct Role of Oxygen Vacancies Not Clearly Demonstrated: Although XPS and EPR characterizations suggest the presence of oxygen vacancies, no control experiments (e.g., synthesizing HTiNbO5-x membranes without oxygen vacancies) were conducted to confirm their necessity. Without such experiments, it is impossible to rule out the dominant role of other factors, such as surface acid sites or differences in interlayer mass transport.
b. Lack of Empirical Evidence for Orbital Symmetry Matching: The manuscript claims that HOMO-LUMO symmetry matching (Fig. 1j) is responsible for the accelerated reaction, but no direct evidence (e.g., in situ spectroscopy such as Raman or XAS) is provided. Reliance solely on DFT calculations is insufficient to support this key mechanistic claim.
2. Unclear Theoretical Model Construction
a. Questionable Validity of the Confined Reaction Model: The differences between the DFT models for "confined reaction" and "bulk reaction" are not clearly explained. For instance, when the interlayer spacing is reduced to 4 Å, how is the model's consistency with the actual material structure (e.g., oxygen vacancy distribution, surface functional groups) ensured? Are solvation effects or dynamic adsorption processes considered?
b. Discrepancy Between Computational Parameters and Experimental Conditions: The manuscript does not clarify whether the interlayer spacings used in the calculations (e.g., 40 Å vs. 4 Å) correspond to the experimentally measured XRD data (e.g., 11.0 Å). If the model parameters do not match the experimental conditions, the computational results lose their explanatory power.
3. Limitations in Material Characterization and Reactor Design
a. Lack of Verification of Interlayer Spacing Uniformity: While SEM and XRD data suggest an ordered layered structure, high-resolution characterization (e.g., HAADF-STEM) is needed to confirm the local uniformity of nanosheet stacking. Stacking defects or interlayer inhomogeneity could significantly affect the reproducibility of the reaction.
b. Mass Transport Effects Not Excluded: The experimental results (e.g., the relationship between reaction time and interlayer spacing) may be dominated by mass transport rates rather than catalytic activity. Additional experiments (e.g., varying flow rates at fixed interlayer spacing) are needed to distinguish the contributions of mass transport and catalysis.

### Reviewer 3

The authors reported the creation of a HTiNbO5-x membrane for esterification of benzyl alcohol with acetic anhydride to yield benzyl acetate and other derivatives (depending on type of benzyl alcohol used). Comprehensive and complementary characterisation techniques were used to provide robust evidence that demonstrated the noteworthy esterification rates and turnover numbers. The mechanism underpinning delivery of such results were evaluated using suitable simulation methodology. Although the research and work merits publication in Nature Communication, there was a major flaw in the design of the experiments. The following questions and comments outline my concerns about experimental design associated with this paper:
1) What is the motivation to develop a membrane for esterification of benzyl alcohol? Existing methods are already well-established and effective. Hence it was unclear why this work is important scientifically or industrially. The only segment of the manuscript that compared the performance of the current membranes with other catalysts was only limited to Lines 230 to 236. There were no analyses on why their membranes are better than existing catalysts beyond catalysis performance.
2) Benzyl alcohol esterification is a well-established process in industry. However, why did the authors not compare outcomes from this work with already established processes? Comparisons were made with catalysts reported in scientific research (mostly used in labs) for e.g., ionic liquids, solid and inorganic acids, but there was no comparison with industrial processes. After all, the authors are in the opinion that their membranes outperform existing methods for benzyl alcohol esterification.
3) Why did the authors use acetonitrile as the solvent and acetic anhydride for esterification in this work? BA is typically esterified in industry using acetic acid (as solvent and reagent for esterification), toluene, or hexane.
4) Are the membranes single use? What is the cyclic catalytic performance of the membranes reported here?
The authors should carefully address these questions to improve the quality of the manuscript that is underpinned by solid, and interesting results before it can be published in Nat. Commun.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Fang et al. present a laminar membrane reactor using HTiNbO5-X nanosheets enriched with oxygen vacancies. This study demonstrates high catalytic performance for the esterification of benzyl alcohol under mild conditions, achieving nearly 100% conversion within 26.6 seconds at 23°C, with a high turnover number of 306.42. The combination of oxygen vacancies and spatial confinement enhances reactant adsorption, improves orbital symmetry matching, and lowers the reaction’s energy barrier, as confirmed by both experimental results and DFT calculations. Additionally, the membrane reactor exhibits long-term stability, maintaining high conversion efficiency over 13 days of continuous use, highlighting its potential for practical applications. Overall, this is an interesting paper, but the following comments and questions should be addressed before this work can be considered for publication in Nature Communications:
• The introduction provides a good background on catalytic materials and the advantages of 2D materials. However, it would be helpful to clearly define the study’s specific objectives and key research questions—particularly regarding the synergistic effects of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement.
• Some technical terms, such as Brønsted acid site modulation and orbital symmetry matching, could benefit from brief explanations for clarity, considering Nature Communications’ broad audience.
• While the DFT analysis is insightful, could the authors also include a kinetic model in Figure 1 that explicitly outlines the rate-limiting steps? This would enhance the mechanistic understanding.
• The manuscript mentions the synergistic effect of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement but doesn’t discuss the actual mechanism. Could the authors provide a more detailed discussion on how these factors influence adsorption, orbital symmetry matching, and energy barrier reduction? A schematic diagram illustrating the proposed mechanism would be beneficial.
• The authors should specify the exact conditions (temperature, duration, and concentration) used in the acid etching and exfoliation steps.
• Have the authors explored regeneration methods after deactivation (e.g., washing or thermal treatment)?
• The comparison with literature values is useful, but a direct catalytic activity comparison (e.g., turnover frequency) against commercial catalysts would strengthen the study’s industrial relevance. Additionally, how does this membrane reactor compare with previously reported catalytic systems such as COFs and LDHs in terms of reaction rates, TOF, and catalyst stability?
• The presented DFT results suggest that decreasing the interlayer distance improves conversion. Have the authors attempted to reduce the interlayer spacing below 11.0 Å?
• The authors should report their synthesis reproducibility (and batch-to-batch variation).
• What is the distribution of the amorphous vs. crystalline phase percentage in the final nanosheets?
• A discussion on how the distribution of Brønsted and Lewis acid sites impacts catalytic performance would be beneficial.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript proposes a concept of using stacked two-dimensional (2D) amorphous/crystalline HTiNbO5−x nanosheets as sub-nanoconfined membrane reactors for the efficient synthesis of acetate ester flavors under mild conditions. The experimental results demonstrate that the esterification of benzyl alcohol achieves nearly 100% conversion within 26.6 seconds when the interlayer spacing is reduced to 11.0 Å, significantly outperforming conventional bulk reactions. The concept has been reported in the previous work (Adv. Mater. 2024, 36, 2310954; Matter 2023, 6, 1173; Adv. Sci. 2024, 11, 2308388). The manuscript suffers from significant shortcomings in mechanistic explanations, model construction, and experimental validation, which undermine the support for its core scientific claims. As it stands, the manuscript is not suitable for publication.
Detailed Comments
1. Insufficient Mechanistic Explanation and Lack of Direct Evidence
The authors attribute the enhanced performance to the synergistic effect of oxygen vacancies and sub-nanoscale confinement. However, the following issues remain unresolved:
a. Direct Role of Oxygen Vacancies Not Clearly Demonstrated: Although XPS and EPR characterizations suggest the presence of oxygen vacancies, no control experiments (e.g., synthesizing HTiNbO5-x membranes without oxygen vacancies) were conducted to confirm their necessity. Without such experiments, it is impossible to rule out the dominant role of other factors, such as surface acid sites or differences in interlayer mass transport.
b. Lack of Empirical Evidence for Orbital Symmetry Matching: The manuscript claims that HOMO-LUMO symmetry matching (Fig. 1j) is responsible for the accelerated reaction, but no direct evidence (e.g., in situ spectroscopy such as Raman or XAS) is provided. Reliance solely on DFT calculations is insufficient to support this key mechanistic claim.
2. Unclear Theoretical Model Construction
a. Questionable Validity of the Confined Reaction Model: The differences between the DFT models for "confined reaction" and "bulk reaction" are not clearly explained. For instance, when the interlayer spacing is reduced to 4 Å, how is the model's consistency with the actual material structure (e.g., oxygen vacancy distribution, surface functional groups) ensured? Are solvation effects or dynamic adsorption processes considered?
b. Discrepancy Between Computational Parameters and Experimental Conditions: The manuscript does not clarify whether the interlayer spacings used in the calculations (e.g., 40 Å vs. 4 Å) correspond to the experimentally measured XRD data (e.g., 11.0 Å). If the model parameters do not match the experimental conditions, the computational results lose their explanatory power.
3. Limitations in Material Characterization and Reactor Design
a. Lack of Verification of Interlayer Spacing Uniformity: While SEM and XRD data suggest an ordered layered structure, high-resolution characterization (e.g., HAADF-STEM) is needed to confirm the local uniformity of nanosheet stacking. Stacking defects or interlayer inhomogeneity could significantly affect the reproducibility of the reaction.
b. Mass Transport Effects Not Excluded: The experimental results (e.g., the relationship between reaction time and interlayer spacing) may be dominated by mass transport rates rather than catalytic activity. Additional experiments (e.g., varying flow rates at fixed interlayer spacing) are needed to distinguish the contributions of mass transport and catalysis.

### Reviewer 3

The authors reported the creation of a HTiNbO5-x membrane for esterification of benzyl alcohol with acetic anhydride to yield benzyl acetate and other derivatives (depending on type of benzyl alcohol used). Comprehensive and complementary characterisation techniques were used to provide robust evidence that demonstrated the noteworthy esterification rates and turnover numbers. The mechanism underpinning delivery of such results were evaluated using suitable simulation methodology. Although the research and work merits publication in Nature Communication, there was a major flaw in the design of the experiments. The following questions and comments outline my concerns about experimental design associated with this paper:
1) What is the motivation to develop a membrane for esterification of benzyl alcohol? Existing methods are already well-established and effective. Hence it was unclear why this work is important scientifically or industrially. The only segment of the manuscript that compared the performance of the current membranes with other catalysts was only limited to Lines 230 to 236. There were no analyses on why their membranes are better than existing catalysts beyond catalysis performance.
2) Benzyl alcohol esterification is a well-established process in industry. However, why did the authors not compare outcomes from this work with already established processes? Comparisons were made with catalysts reported in scientific research (mostly used in labs) for e.g., ionic liquids, solid and inorganic acids, but there was no comparison with industrial processes. After all, the authors are in the opinion that their membranes outperform existing methods for benzyl alcohol esterification.
3) Why did the authors use acetonitrile as the solvent and acetic anhydride for esterification in this work? BA is typically esterified in industry using acetic acid (as solvent and reagent for esterification), toluene, or hexane.
4) Are the membranes single use? What is the cyclic catalytic performance of the membranes reported here?
The authors should carefully address these questions to improve the quality of the manuscript that is underpinned by solid, and interesting results before it can be published in Nat. Commun.

Sub-nanometer-confined reaction is the ultimate frontier of catalytic chemistry, yet it is
challenging to form the angstrom channels with distributed atomic catalytic centers
within. Herein, amorphous/crystalline HTiNbO nanosheets with abundant oxygen
5-X
vacancy were successfully prepablue and stacked as 2D sub-nanoconfined membrane
flow reactors. The Brønsted acid sites and oxygen vacancies are engineeblue onto the
HTiNbO nanosheets by acid etching. The synergy of multiple sites and confined
5-X
spatial structures are realized in this laminar membrane reactor. Up to now, no works
regarding these factors associates for organic reaction tuning have been reported. Thus,
this work is important scientifically.
The esterification of alcohols with acetic anhydride is used as a model reaction, because
it is a conversion of both environmental and industrial importance. Conventionally, the
esterification of benzyl alcohol with acetic acid or acetic anhydride is performed in the
presence of mineral acids catalysts (e.g., H SO ). However, the inherent disadvantages
2 4
related with the homogeneous system lie in separation and purification of the products,
resulting in the environmental problems and economical inconveniences. Over the past
few decades, various catalytic materials or systems have been exploblue to replace
mineral acids (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2009, 48, 168-171; Nat. Commun. 2014, 5, 3170;
Adv. Mater. 2025, 37, 2413949; J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2023, 145, 15680-15687). In this
work, we report an outstanding laminar membrane reactors. The Brønsted acid sites and
oxygen vacancies are engineeblue into the 2D sub-nanoconfined channels.
Consequently, the membrane reactor exhibits ≈ 100% conversion from benzyl alcohol
to benzyl acetate within 26.6 s at 23 °C and 28 times higher TON than that of bulk
reaction, and also shows satisfactory performance to other alcohol derivatives. This
strategy can provide a reference to other 2D materials and organic synthesis reactions.
Thus, this work has the potential for industrial applications.
